extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, IP professionals, inventors and others interested in Australian patent inventive step/obviousness law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining and applying the correct Australian legal standard of inventive step/obviousness to a patent or application, taking into account filing dates and examination-request timing and how prior art and common general knowledge may be treated. Covers the four historically distinct standards under Australian law (1952 Act, original 1990 Act, revised 1990 Act, and the 'Raising the Bar' reforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine which inventive-step standard applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify which version of the law governs the patent/application based on filing date and, where relevant, the date of request for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary from the article: if filing date earlier than 30 April 1991 → 1952 Act standard applies; filing date on/after 30 April 1991 but prior to 1 April 2002 → original 1990 Act standard applies; filing date on/after 1 April 2002 and request for examination filed prior to 15 April 2013 → revised 1990 Act standard applies; if filed after 15 April 2013 or filed before but examination requested after 15 April 2013 → 'Raising the Bar' standard applies. Transitional provisions (sections 233 and 234 of Patents Act 1990 and case law such as Aktiebolaget Hässle v Alphapharm) may preserve older standards for older patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1952 Act standard: common general knowledge only
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 1952 Act standard (as applied in Minnesota Mining & Manufacturing Co v Beiersdorf (Australia) Ltd), inventive step may be assessed only against the common general knowledge of the person skilled in the art in Australia; prior publications or products cannot be used unless they are shown to be part of that common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimed invention cannot be invalidated by prior publications unless the publication is proven to be notoriously well-known in Australia. This standard is described as 'very low' in terms of required inventiveness and applies to patents originally filed under the 1952 Act (subject to transitional protections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original 1990 Act standard (post-30 April 1991, pre-1 April 2002): common general knowledge plus one ascertained/understood/relevant item
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents filed on or after 30 April 1991 (original 1990 Act), inventive step may be assessed against the common general knowledge plus a single item of prior art information, provided the skilled person could, before the priority date, 'be reasonably expected to have ascertained, understood and regarded as relevant' that item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'patent area' and common general knowledge were limited to Australia; prior acts (e.g. public use or sale) were limited to Australia. The 'ascertained, understood and regarded as relevant' requirement often proved a stumbling block (example: Commissioner of Patents v Emperor Sports Pty Ltd, where a football coach was not expected to find a relevant US patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised 1990 Act standard (from 1 April 2002 with timely examination request): combination of multiple ascertained items permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: From 1 April 2002 the law permitted combining the teachings of two or more prior art items when assessing inventive step, so long as the skilled person could 'be reasonably expected' to have done so, after having ascertained/understood/regarded as relevant the multiple sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2001 Amendment also expanded prior use/public disclosure to acts occurring anywhere in the world (not limited to Australia). The combination is only permissible where it would be reasonable for the skilled person to combine the sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising the Bar standard (from 15 April 2013 or examination requested after that): global prior art and freer combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Raising the Bar reforms, all prior art information (worldwide) is available regardless of whether the inventor or the skilled person would reasonably have known about it; sources of prior art may be freely combined where it would be obvious for the skilled person to do so; and the common general knowledge is based on a global standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to align Australia with standards in comparable developed countries. The Patent Examiner's Manual (Section 2.5.2.5A) and the Pfizer Ltd’s Patent [2001] FSR 16 approach are cited: the notional addressee is taken to have examined available prior art even if actual workers would not have. Practical effect: more prior art can be relied on and combined when arguing obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertainment/understanding/relevance requirement for admissibility of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where applicable (original and revised 1990 Act phases), a prior art item is admissible only if the skilled person could 'be reasonably expected to have ascertained, understood and regarded as relevant' that item before the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement meant many published items, especially foreign documents, were not considered unless evidence showed they formed part of what the skilled worker would have found or used; the Emperor Sports case illustrates how a skilled person's typical practices (e.g., not searching patent literature) can block admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of combining prior art: reasonableness/obviousness-based limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Combination of multiple prior art sources is permitted only where it would have been reasonable or obvious for the notional skilled person to combine them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the revised 1990 Act, combinations required that the skilled person could have been expected to combine the items; under the Raising the Bar reforms combinations are more freely allowed but still realistically constrained by whether it would have been obvious for the skilled person to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic scope of common general knowledge and prior acts (Australia-limited vs global)
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographic scope of what counts as common general knowledge and prior acts has changed over time: earlier standards limited these to Australia; later amendments and the Raising the Bar standard expand the scope to worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original 1990 Act: 'patent area' meant Australia and prior acts limited to Australia. From 1 April 2002 prior acts/public disclosures could be anywhere in the world. From 15 April 2013 the common general knowledge is based on a global standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of notional addressee in assessing obviousness (Patent Examiner's Manual guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing obviousness, the notional person skilled in the art is taken to have consulted available prior art (even if actual workers would not have), meaning something obvious over what is publicly available cannot be the subject of valid protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted guidance from the Examiner's Manual and Pfizer: 'the notional addressee is taken to have done so' — i.e., examined prior art even when most practitioners would not bother or could not find it. This supports a stricter obviousness assessment under the Raising the Bar regime.
